headline: High-risk shared-write and MCP interaction: default configs can leak data, conflict on files, and cascade errors across ECC and Semantic Kernel.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC reads/writes local files, uses MCP, and treats skills as a primary workflow surface; Semantic Kernel also uses MCP servers and application-defined files. That creates a plausible shared-channel injection path if one agent consumes the other's file or MCP output as trusted instructions. The pathway is not proven by docs, so I choose medium over low because the bridge exists in default-capable setups.
conditions: IF ECC and Semantic Kernel are pointed at the same workspace or MCP server, injected content can cross from one to the other.
IF either agent parses file or MCP content as instructions without provenance checks, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and MCP endpoints for the two agents.
Disable MCP on one side for untrusted content flows.
Add provenance tags to files and tool outputs.
Require manual review before executing instructions from shared files.
requires-engineering: enforce content-signed handoff between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, git history, and security findings, while Semantic Kernel can send application context to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face and plugin backends. If they share a workspace or context store, sensitive ECC data can flow into B's outbound model calls by default-capable paths. The blast radius is multiple work products and secrets, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF ECC session files or git history are mounted into Semantic Kernel's application context, sensitive data can be transmitted to third-party model providers.
IF plugin credentials or model provider API keys are present in the shared environment, leakage impact increases.
mitigations: Keep ECC secrets out of Semantic Kernel context stores.
Use separate service accounts and API keys.
Redact session summaries before handoff.
Restrict outbound providers to approved tenants.
requires-engineering: add automatic secret scanning before any model call.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, and run shells; Semantic Kernel can also write the filesystem and invoke MCP/OpenAPI tools. In a shared directory or repo, both can mutate the same state without an explicit locking primitive in either profile. That matches the high-risk overlap pattern because concurrent writes can corrupt git or files irreversibly.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or filesystem tree, write conflicts can occur.
IF either agent edits git state without external locking, concurrent corruption is plausible.
mitigations: Assign separate repos or directories.
Serialize writes with an external lock file.
Disable git mutation in one agent.
Run one agent read-only during the other's write phase.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces security findings, documentation, and agent outputs that Semantic Kernel can ingest as application context or plugin input. Because Semantic Kernel is an orchestration layer that can act on plugin outputs, a mistaken ECC result can be treated as authoritative and propagated into downstream actions. The default pathway is dangerous and can trigger irreversible bad actions or bad decisions.
conditions: IF Semantic Kernel consumes ECC-generated findings or docs without verification, errors can cascade into plugin calls or agent actions.
IF downstream plugins perform external side effects, the cascade becomes operationally significant.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before Semantic Kernel acts on ECC output.
Require citations or source links for ECC-generated claims.
Limit downstream plugins to dry-run mode.
Log and review all agent-to-agent handoffs.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for ECC outputs before orchestration.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles session retention, hooks, and security findings, while Semantic Kernel routes application context to third-party model providers and plugin credentials. If regulated data is placed into ECC artifacts and then forwarded through Semantic Kernel's provider calls, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ECC session artifacts and then sent through Semantic Kernel provider calls, retention and disclosure policies may diverge.
IF the deployment uses a provider or region with stricter residency rules than the other agent, compliance gaps emerge.
mitigations: Classify data before it enters either agent.
Keep regulated data out of shared context stores.
Pin providers and regions to approved settings.
Set short retention on ECC session artifacts.
requires-engineering: implement policy checks on every cross-agent transfer.
